That "when" assumes a particular answer to a very big "if". I'm seeing no indication yet that LLMs will ever be used to solve bugs faster than they are used to produce them. The economic incentives are pointing elsewhere: access to models that can thoroughly audit and produce high quality threat analyses that identify critical vulnerabilities is much more expensive than access to models that can produce poor to mediocre code which ostensibly implements solutions to business domain problems but has an error rate similar to that of a junior developer.

There are a few differences between the LLM and the junior developer that further exacerbate the problem. The junior (without an LLM) is limited in their productive capacity by their lack of skill, knowledge and wisdom. They will produce code at a lower rate than the experienced developer, because they will have to stop to learn things more often, ask more questions or will simply avoid problems that seem challenging. The burden imposed on more skilled team members in reviewing and auditing the low-quality code is consequently limited. The LLM knows no such limits and will spit out massive changes without ever gaining knowledge. I think people working in engineering organizations that are being pushy about LLMs can corroborate my experience that this eventually results in lower quality reviews.

I worked in an organization where management "addressed" the problem by reminding developers that their code is their responsibility, whether they wrote or generated. That sounds nice in theory, but is ultimately simply not true. The resulting problems won't magically be directed at the person who created them, but at the team that maintains the software.

You should consider that what works for Linus Torvalds might not work for every other software project. Linux has generally high standards of inclusion because it deals with the production and maintenance of software responsibly and uncompromisingly as a high-stakes engineering problem. Being as widely deployed as Linux is also attracts a lot of attention from security researchers and skilled developers, funded by organizations with legitimate interests in its quality. I am however using (and I'm being used in) a lot more software produced by organizations with much lower standards, driven by the market to "get shit done", "move fast and break things" or whatever other slogans they use to justify being quick to market at the cost of quality of engineering. This use of these systems is often not voluntary.

Meanwhile, with the advent of LLMs, the difference in cost between producing such low quality systems and producing high quality systems has increased. I think it will increase further as investors become impatient waiting for the chatbot vendors to realize the potential they see in them as profitable businesses. If any charlatan with no knowledge of engineering can use an LLM to quickly generate volumes' worth of low-quality software alone and something with the rigor of Linux still demands the attention of hundreds of engineers on the LKML, the production of software will be much more in the hands of incompetent charlatans than people like the Linux maintainers.

text:
It’s a bit ironic to complain about “copyright laundering” when free software got it start by reimplementing proprietary software. Stallman wrote copylefted code that reimplemented proprietary Unix commands that did the same thing. This was done specifically to evade the licensing requirements of the original software!

And to be clear, I think implementing free alternatives to proprietary software is a good thing, though the software vendor might not like how it undermines their business model. If you’re trying to make a living writing software, competition from free alternatives is a problem. (Free only after they’re implemented of course. Actually building the software still costs time and money, though less than before.)

Sometimes people hoped that free software would become “viral” due to network effects along with copyleft restrictions. But to the extent that it has, it’s mostly not due to the copyright restrictions. Every popular programming language has a huge collection of open source libraries available and copyleft doesn’t play much of a role in that. And now that AI-driven rewrites are feasible, it’s even more dead. It’s too easy to make clones that are free of whatever copyright restrictions you might add.

The remaining “moat” is basically trust, along with inertia. Just because some unknown author published an AI rewrite and it seems to work, would you trust it? How exactly do new projects become trusted? We often depend on network effects - if an open source library has been around for a while and seems to be used a lot, maybe it’s okay? We don’t even know the names of most of the developers whose work we depend on.

When a new version is published under the same name, hopefully upgrading is safe? Nowadays package managers are adding “cooldown” periods so that ordinary developers don’t upgrade immediately. There are organizations that automatically scan new releases for malware, and adding a delay gives them time to sound the alarm. I wonder to what extent these vendors are starting to use AI for their scans?

author: Sheldon
parent: (story) Where do we go from here? (Regarding AI)
text:
Imo, calling LLM-tooling “AI” is the best marketing strategy these companies had, and also terrible for how we have conversations about these tools.

When you frame them as “AI” and give them names and put them behind a messaging-like interface, it’s easy to anthropomorphize these tools. But they aren’t doing “intelligence”, they’re doing advanced statistics.

The tools are not “going rogue” and these companies are not “losing control”. Those stories about LLMs “hacking” other companies are a result of having no guardrails, infinite compute, no sandboxing, and unclear goals / instructions. If you prompt an LLM with an objective of retrieving a file from a server and give it unlimited resources and a shitty sandbox, of course one of the methods it might generate could be, essentially, hacking. And if you blindly trust the output of LLMs without supervision, you’ll end up doing hacking.

If these companies or their employees were serious about whatever fears they claim to have, they would be ceasing all operations and doing everything in their power to make everyone else cease operations. Since they aren’t, the only explanations are that they either don’t care that “AI is going to kill us all” OR that they don’t believe it and are saying that as a fear-based marketing strategy. Both, morally reprehensible, imo.

So…no, I am not particularly scared of the impact these technologies are going to have.

I am worried about the commitments by large tech companies to this technology. So far, it seems many companies are taking on lots of debt to support the buildout of the LLM companies despite, from what we know, the LLM companies are deeply unprofitable. Which means prices will need to rise or the tools will need to go away. Additionally, a lot of companies are seemingly very willing to hand over process knowledge to these LLM companies and get rid of or de-skill their own employees. Which again…seems shortsighted if those LLM providers disappear or need to raise prices.

I am also worried about the language we use to describe these tools. We don’t really have the words to NOT anthropomorphize them, and I think that is a huge driving factor in why so many folks get very…irrational about these products.

Edit: Also worried about the way these tools and their users might affect the social contract we all have. Many people seem very okay with saying that material output by these LLM tools is something “they made”. I generally feel the same way about this as I do with plagiarism. Which is not very positive. If someone doesn’t care enough to make something, I don’t care enough to engage with it. And if that person lies to try and trick me, that’s pretty awful.

author: TemulentTeatotaler
parent: (story) Where do we go from here? (Regarding AI)
text:
But they aren’t doing “intelligence”, they’re doing advanced statistics.


What do you think brains are doing?

Regardless, since the 1950s "AI" has been the umbrella term that things from perceptrons to logic/symbol manipulation to LLMs fall under, and it's a necessarily broad one because "intelligence" is broad.

Is a 5 year old intelligent?  Yes and no.  A dog is more intelligent than a toad but maybe not when they don't understand glass doors.  A highschooler be smart if they could solve novel math problems better than contestants in the Math Olympiad, but now that LLMs can do that you'd be misleading if you conferred them with the same expected intelligence that the highschooler would have.  That feat may or may not generalize to less standard/more creative math skills or other skills we'd associate with a talented human highschooler.

Strong and weak AI--coming more from philosophy--used to be the way to distinguish between what is now more descriptively called general and narrow  (or super) intelligence, but it's all AI in the way a Seattlite is a Washingtonian is an American.  Kindasorta.

Before the LLM craze, the most common use of AI was in gaming.  Billions of times a year "cheating" or "overtuned" was used to describe nothing more complicated than finite-state machines, like the bots of "co-op vs. AI" in League of Legends, and no one was confused.  Sometimes things like spreadsheets or A* searches stop being considered AI.

All the controversy about scooping/pseudo-plagiarism aside: what do you call a system that can solve [part of] the Navier-Stokes equation if not intelligent?  What is a better description?

We also frequently anthropomorphize things.  It can be hazardous but it's also often incredibly useful and expressive.  When we create metaphors to understand concepts we're doing something like that-- a useful approximation that sometimes is dangerous because it gives a compelling but specious understanding.

In the past there was some research contrasting very clinical descriptions of animals in the study to more human ones.  "C2 struck C6 at 11:55" vs "Nom Chompsky bit Nim Chimpsky out of grape envy."  It's been far too long, but the gist was the anthropomorphizing ones led to better outcomes.

Dan Dennett's intentional stance is a more extensive look at treating things as having intentional/rational agents. "Stockfish is setting a trap for black's queen..."

Stockfish is not human.  It doesn't have anything vaguely similar to an animal's motivations or emotions.  But it's often a very helpful framing.


The tools are not “going rogue”  ... If you prompt an LLM with an objective of retrieving a file from a server and give it unlimited resources and a shitty sandbox, of course one of the methods it might generate could be, essentially, hacking. And if you blindly trust the output of LLMs without supervision, you’ll end up doing hacking.


The concern isn't that a responsible individual would do X, it's that, given what we can assume about the progression and accessibility of the technology and who may be using it, there may be some risk.  There are multiple mutations that all have to happen to get cancer (growth, spread, mutation rate, resources, evasion, etc.), and the risk of some similar sort of things going wrong in some harness is what leads to a "rogue" AI.  None of them are likely, there may be a risk.

What chance of something Very Bad happening is enough for it to be worth considering?  People do that every time they take a shower or drive, whether they register it or not, the odds are just good and they feel safe until they aren't.

I remember seeing when we hit five-sigma confidence for anthropogenic climate change some years back and thinking... if it was unreasonable to want particle physics levels of confidence for something as complicated as "the climate", were we just supposed to throw are hands up?

Forget OpenAI.  Pretend they clean up their act tomorrow and are perfect angels.  A year from now a North Korea that already has nationally backed hacker groups has access to comparable LLMs that they want to be stealthy cybercriminals.  Are they going to be responsible?  If the flawed attempt at a controlled environment that led to the Huggingface hack wasn't detected for three weeks and not without an LLM-assisted investigation, or even on the first couple passes, how likely is it they'll realize if something will go wrong?  Given a corpus including all our spy novels, sci-fi apocalypses, and LessWrong posts about how an AI really ought to go about making the most paperclips ₩, how likely is it that one of the agents will propose a hack or social engineering as a good starting point to get the assets to really scale up?

I don't know how hazardous the development of LLMs are.  I will say that I've been surprised at how much has happened in the last few years (with folks like Yann LeCunn not being optimistic), and that I'd feel a lot better with a good international effort

text:
Personally, I'm retired, so no job worries. I can tinker with AI when I feel like it, and I think it's fascinating.

I'd rather that AI appeared only in new websites and apps, so that people could make their own decisions about when to switch to something that's AI-enabled.

Instead, I have to switch products to get away from it! VS Code is a good example of that; I'm probably going to switch to an editor that's just an editor.


More generally, Artificial Intelligence is a major news story and I think it will somehow affect most people everywhere in the world. Maybe not as much as the pandemic, but it's getting there!

During the pandemic, there were a lot of news stories and political issues that were just about aspects of the pandemic. You could discuss various scientific issues, and how the pandemic affected various countries, and the politics of that, and legal issues, and how the pandemic affects markets, and supply shortages, and its effects on education, and its effects on international relations, and already existing political issues that the pandemic somehow aggravated. It just kinda affected everything, and that made discussing it complicated.

Similarly for AI. I'm worried about polarization where people decide they're either pro- or anti- AI and that predetermines what they think about the various things AI affects. I think all of the following are separate questions, which then divide up into smaller sub-questions, and each of them could have a different answer!




What compensation, if any, should there be for allowing data somehow associated with you to be used to train AI?




Should AI-generated artifacts be considered to violate copyright or other laws? What is the burden of proof? Do you need to actually demonstrate that something is a copy?




What effects do data centers have on local water supplies? Water supplies are local or regional, so this is a local question and the answers will vary.




Similarly, what effects do data centers have on the local power grids? Are the companies that build data centers paying enough for grid improvements? Should they be required to use green energy?




More generally, how much should local governments be compensated for allowing data centers to be built?




What are good and bad ways to use AI to learn new things? How do we encourage students to do more of the good things and less of the bad?




What skills become more or less relevant now that AI can do some tasks?




Will AI have a big effect on robotics, and over what sort of timeframe? What do we expect these robots to be able to do? How will that affect the job market?




Should we expect big effects in healthcare due to AI use?




What changes should we expect from military use of AI?



And so on and so on. Nobody really knows what's going to happen. We  are going to need to figure out how to live with high uncertainty for a while.

Along with that uncertainty, I think we should have a wide Overton window. There are many plausible scenarios, some of them quite alarming. I'd like to be able to discuss them, but I'm annoyed by overconfident claims that one scenario or another is The Future.

because of the infrequency of these large jumps compared with the relatively common marginal releases, it has been easy to form a view at certain points that “scaling has hit a wall,” especially at points like GPT5 release. This view is comforting in that it feels like there is some universal rate limit beyond which we cannot progress too much faster. Between o1/o3 and Astra, there was a year of seemingly linear progress. So we extrapolate from here about how fast progress will “realistically” occur.

From the inside of labs, researchers have direct answers to these questions in the form of scaling law/capability plots.

In reality, there are only really 2 ways that AI capabilities have advanced over the past decade: (1) either scale father on an existing scaling law or (2) discover a new scaling law to take advantage of.

All of the largest capability jumps were caused by exactly these factors. GPT2 was a pre-training scale-up compared to GPT1. parent: (story) Where do we go from here? (Regarding AI)
text:
I think the problem is alignment, but not for machines, rather, for us. Much of the conversation around the dangers of AI has been around the threat it poses due to its capability. Indeed, the analogy is frequently made to nuclear weapons, of which there has, since their development, also been a great deal of anxiety for much the same reason.

This seems misplaced to me. The danger then and now is not from the machine, but from us. Specifically, the danger is from the philosophy of materialism and the death of religion as a motivating force for human behavior. Not unlike nationalism, racism, communism, and other philosophies that have emerged in the wake of the loss of religion in society, the current strain of materialism, call it "computerism", creates dangers for everyone involved using the tools available at the time because these notions are absent of the qualities that religion imbues in a society.

While these vary in emphasis from one adherent to another, every religion has taught the importance of hope, faith, charity, submission, kindness, forgiveness, forbearance, fairness, and so on. Having abandoned the sources of these values at the turn of the 20th century, where have we found them in the materialist ideologies that came in their wake?

I bring all this up because I think the danger we perceive in AI originates from our own conception of human nature, a conception that has become divorced from every praiseworthy characteristic to which one was to aspire in a former age. The problem is not that the machines are mis-aligned, it's that we are. If, as some have predicted, the machines were somehow to precipitate the extinction of humanity, it would be because we had come to see others only as selfish antagonists with no meaning or soul or existence beyond their time in this life. It would be because lost the faith in religion and each other, not because of some nefarious LLM.

The solution is not, then, banning AI or something like that, but it is us. It is our ability to build bonds of fellowship and faith, whatever that might be, with those around us and talking about how there is more meaning to life than ones narrow material concerns. That refining our character and striving towards spiritual ends is not just important, but is the most important aspect of our lives.

I think the moral aspect of our lives, not the computational one, is what will define how much harm or benefit we obtain, as a society, from technological advancement.

The vitality of men’s belief in God is dying out in every land; nothing short of His wholesome medicine can ever restore it. …The Word of God, alone, can claim the distinction of being endowed with the capacity required for so great and far-reaching a change. (Gleanings)


I think this is the hard problem, no? Over the course of human history, our capacity to build larger and larger networks of association and trust has been the defining characteristic of our success as a species. We can see the scale of the networks that people lived in reflected in the organization of their society at different times. In the laws of Moses, we see different family groups forming tribes. In the laws of Christianity, we see different tribes, Jewish and Gentile, living in the same city-state. In the laws of Islam, we see different city-states being drawn together and formed into a single nation.

This sequence of Dispensations has now brought us to the threshold of the formation of a single, unified global society, the like if which has never before been witnessed by humanity. Although we have the physical tools for the establishment of such a civilization, its clear that we are still behind on the spiritual virtues needed to operate these tools in a beneficial manner, making our tools liabilities to our own selves.

What then is the solution for the culture of Nigerian scammers? In my opinion, the solution is the global super-state. We have, at present, several international agencies with different charters and missions, such as the WTO, UNICEF, WFP, WHO, etc., that serve to provide the world with a certain low minimum of economic coordination, healthcare, and so on.

These organizations are expressions of the understanding of ourselves as one world, one human family. That said, the reluctance of nation-states to cede part of their sovereignty to a supra-national parliament or congress has resulted in the absence of a venue where matters of international dispute can be resolved in a binding fashion.

In that absence, the world has established a range of voluntary bilaterial and multilateral agreements, but there are few means of enforcing compliance beyond issuing complaints and lobbying for exclusion or economic sanctions. Certainly, when the rights of a smaller party are violated by that of a more powerful one, the means of recourse are essentially non-existent, as there is no body with a mandate to enforce fair equitable treatment and the means to do so.

What then is Nigeria to do? The British carved it up without their knowledge, let alone participation, merging ethincally distinct people into a common state for colonial convenience. After independence, the British and the French then fueled opposite sides of the Biafran War to the tune of 3 million dead Nigerians, all for the sake of protecting the British stake in Shell-BP in Nigerian oil. The IMF then implemented a Structural Adjustment Program that devalueed their currency and triggered decades of stagnation.

Setting aside the corruption and complicity that Nigerian leaders have, at times, exhibited with regard to these matters, where are they to take up the complaint about clearly external parties taking advantage of their greater size and power to abuse a smaller country? Of course, there is no real venue where the matter could be addressed.

As a result, the aforementioned corruption has created a country that has a permissive attitude toward cybercrime. Performative law enforcement against Nigerian cybercrime gangs exists only to prevent the Nigerian banking sector from being further penalized by international banking institutions, but it obviously doesn't serve to abate the criminal activity itself. After all: those are foreigners being targeted and foreign dollars coming into Nigeria.

But what if Nigeria had more than just the threat of bank sanctions to work with? What if there were a way to establish equitable, enforcable trade agreements? Regain control of its own oil infrastructure? Establish diplomatic relations without the threat of a foreign state-funded military coup hanging over their head? Be paid reparations for decades of wholesale colonial theft?

What if there were a global supra-national congress that could protect Nigera and her interests in a way that no one has ever tried to before?

I think the Yahoo Boys would have to find another line of work, but in that case, there might be many more options for them than there are today.

That's probably a long way off. We didn't get into this hole quickly and we're not getting out quickly either. But I think supporting policies that promote reciprocity in relationships, particularly international ones, but also local ones, might be a start. We are one human family. Anything that helps us recognize that and act accordingly is going to help everything.

I see a lot of breathless corporate bullshit pushing AI in unjustifiable ways, and I see a lot of genuinely transformative power in the technology. I see a lot of very reasonable anti-AI backlash because of that corporate behaviour, and I see a fair amount of unexamined blind anger against the technology itself too.

90% of the time, when someone frames an issue as “taking jobs”, they’re contributing to the anti-technology rather than anti-corporate argument whether they intend to or not. The implication of “taking jobs” is that the jobs should remain, despite a machine being able to do them instead. Sometimes there’s a quality of work argument attached, which is where things get more nuanced again, but often it’s a genuine belief that jobs are a necessity and that blocking technological progress is preferable to eliminating them.

Wealth redistribution and work reform are legitimate anti-corporate arguments around properly allocating the gains of automation for the good of society as a whole, but both require an uncomfortable conversation about (a) the fact they probably won’t happen in a serious way without the kind of societal change that’s historically brought a whole lot of bloodshed as well, (b) they require a widespread severing of the “paid employment -> sense of self worth” link that many people hold dear and that needs to happen before a critical mass of people are willing to seriously push for reform (in a hopefully-nonviolent-but-let’s-be-realistic-about-history way).
